title: Entanglement swapping across a five-node relay in a multiplexed quantum-classical network
authors: Andrew R. Cameron, Jordan M. Thomas, Alexandru Macridin, Si Xie, Raju Valivarthi, Soumya S. Ghosh, Yerko Muñoz Barros, Neil Sinclair, Panagiotis Spentzouris, Maria Spiropulu, Prem Kumar, Cristián Peña
abstract: Quantum networks are resources for scaling quantum computers and distributed sensing technologies while offering post-quantum security benefits. Teleporting non-classical resources like entanglement, via so called entanglement swapping, is essential for networks in particular overcoming rate-loss limits via quantum repeaters. Deploying these systems on real infrastructure will likely require multiplexing photonic qubits into fibers carrying 'classical' light encoding standard Internet communications and control plane signals for multi-node quantum protocols. Here, we report the first demonstration of entanglement swapping and conventional communications operating over the same fibers. Entanglement is swapped across a five-node quantum relay topology connected by four long-distance fibers, each populated with classical data signals. Time-bin entangled photons in the C-band are multiplexed alongside C-band classical signals using dense-wavelength division multiplexing, introducing noise photons generated by high-power classical light. We experimentally and theoretically characterize the trade-off between quantum fidelity and Raman noise photons. Entanglement swapping is demonstrated over a maximum fiber length of 40 km (four 10-km fibers) while simultaneously transmitting 10-Gbps classical data through all fibers. These results represent a significant advancement in the demonstrated complexity of coexisting quantum and classical networks and provide a roadmap for achieving the widespread deployment of advanced quantum technologies.
summary: This paper reports the first experimental demonstration of entanglement swapping across a multi-node quantum relay while simultaneously transmitting high-speed classical data over the same optical fibers. By characterizing the noise introduced by co-propagating classical signals, the authors establish a roadmap for deploying advanced quantum technologies in real-world, noisy communication channels.
main_problem: The primary challenge addressed is demonstrating entanglement swapping and conventional classical communications operating simultaneously over the same optical fibers, which is crucial for real-world quantum network deployment.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated entanglement swapping over 40 km while simultaneously transmitting 10-Gbps classical data, proving the feasibility of coexisting quantum and classical networks.
method: The work combines experimental measurements of entanglement fidelity and noise characterization with theoretical modeling using Gaussian overlap integrals to simulate detection probabilities.
model_or_system: The system involves a five-node quantum relay topology connected by long-distance fibers, utilizing dense-wavelength division multiplexing (DWDM) to co-propagate time-bin entangled photons and high-power classical data signals.
key_observables: Entanglement swapping visibility, quantum fidelity ($F$), and the rate of spontaneous Raman scattering (SpRS) noise photons.
important_parameters: Maximum fiber length of 40 km, simultaneous 10-Gbps classical data transmission, and the trade-off between quantum fidelity and classical launch power.
main_assumptions: The analysis characterizes the trade-off with Raman noise, and simulations explore different wavelength allocations (C/C, O/C, C/O) to mitigate noise effects.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the conceptual setup, detailed experimental architecture, and quantitative results showing visibility and noise rates as a function of classical launch power and fiber length.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the physical necessity of quantum-classical coexistence, detailing the experimental setup and measurements of noise/fidelity, and concluding with theoretical modeling to predict performance limits based on noise sources.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it tackles the engineering challenge of integrating quantum signals into existing classical infrastructure, which is a major bottleneck for scaling quantum networks.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Conceptual diagram of entanglement swapping across a ﬁve-node quantum relay over four ﬁber links wherein higher-power classical communication signals are wavelength-multiplexed in and out of each ﬁber. Two independent entangled photon-pair sources (EPPS) generate entangled photon pairs. One photon from each source is transmitted through a ﬁber segment of length L/4 to a central node for a Bell state measurement (BSM). The other photons from the EPPSs are sent a distance L/4 to either Alice or Bob. A successful BSM at Charlie’s midpoint relay node heralds entanglement between the two remaining photons at Alice’s and Bob’s nodes, despite having never directly interacted.

Figure 2: Detailed experimental architecture for entanglement swapping in a quantum-classical coexistence relay. The setup utilizes a common 1536.6-nm mode-locked laser to pump two independent SPDC sources. Each of the four quantum paths consists of a SMF-28 ﬁber spool with either lengths L = 5 km (20-km total span) or L = 10 km (40-km total span). Each ﬁber segment is populated by wavelength-multiplexed C-band time-bin photons co-propagating with 10-Gbps classical data signals allocated to a neighboring DWDM channel.
